scenes.title: Completing the Square
scenes.promise: Turn any quadratic into the form that hands you its turning point — and proves it can never dip below zero.
scenes.narration: Welcome. In the next few minutes you'll learn one rewrite, completing the square, that turns any quadratic into a form which hands you its turning point on a plate, and lets you prove it never dips below zero.

scenes.heading: Why the ordinary form hides things
scenes.text:
$y = x^2 - 4x$ looks simple, but at a glance it tells you almost nothing: where is its lowest point? What is its smallest value?

The same curve written as $y = (x-2)^2 - 4$ answers both instantly — lowest point $(2, -4)$, smallest value $-4$.

This lesson is the rewrite that takes you from the first form to the second, every time.
scenes.narration: Look at y equals x squared minus four x. It looks simple, but it hides exactly the things exams ask for: where is the lowest point, and what is the smallest value? Write the same curve as x minus two, all squared, minus four, and both answers are sitting right there. This lesson is the rewrite that gets you from one form to the other.

scenes.heading: Same curve, moved about
scenes.caption: Every quadratic is $y = x^2$ moved about. In $y = a(x-h)^2 + k$: the $h$ slides it sideways, the $k$ lifts or drops it, and $a$ stretches it — a negative $a$ flips it upside down. The turning point is always $(h, k)$.
scenes.narration: Watch the curve. Start with y equals x squared. Replace x by x minus two and the whole curve slides two to the right. Take four away and it drops by four. Put a minus in front and it flips upside down. Every quadratic is x squared moved about, and the completed-square form is the record of the moves.

scenes.heading: The form — name the parts
scenes.intro: Completed square form, the shape every answer ends in:

callouts.label: $a > 0$: opens upwards, the turning point is a **minimum**. $a < 0$: opens downwards, a **maximum**.
$h$ is the $x$-coordinate of the turning point — sign trap: $(x+3)^2$ means $h = -3$, not $3$.
$k$ is the maximum or minimum VALUE of $y$. Turning point $(h, k)$ — read it straight off.

scenes.narration: Here's the form every answer ends in: y equals a, bracket x minus h, squared, plus k. The a tells you which way it opens. Positive means a minimum, negative means a maximum. The h is the x-coordinate of the turning point, and here's the trap: x plus three, squared, means h is minus three. And k is the greatest or least value of y. So the turning point is simply h comma k.

scenes.heading: The recipe: half it, square it, add and subtract
scenes.intro: Express $y = x^2 - 3x + 2$ in the form $(x-h)^2 + k$.

steps.note: Half the coefficient of $x$: $-3 \to -\tfrac{3}{2}$. Square it: $\tfrac{9}{4}$. ADD it and SUBTRACT it at once — the value hasn't changed.
The first three terms ARE a perfect square — expand $\left(x - \tfrac{3}{2}\right)^2$ and you get exactly them back.
$-\tfrac{9}{4} + 2 = -\tfrac{1}{4}$. Turning point $\left(\tfrac{3}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{4}\right)$, a minimum — read straight off.

verify.note: the rewrite is the same function

scenes.narration: Here's the recipe. Take the coefficient of x, that's minus three. Halve it: minus three over two. Square it: nine over four. Now add that number and subtract it in the same breath, so nothing has changed. The first three terms are now a perfect square, x minus three over two, all squared. Tidy the leftovers, minus nine over four plus two is minus a quarter, and you're done. The turning point is three over two, minus a quarter.

scenes.heading: When x² has a number in front

steps.note: The recipe only works when $x^2$ has coefficient 1 — so factorize the 2 out of EVERY term first.
Inside the bracket: half of $\tfrac{5}{2}$ is $\tfrac{5}{4}$; square it, add and subtract.
Multiply the 2 back into BOTH terms — leaving $-\tfrac{17}{16}$ alone is the classic slip. Turning point $\left(-\tfrac{5}{4}, -\tfrac{17}{8}\right)$.

verify.note: the rewrite is the same function

scenes.narration: Now the coefficient of x squared isn't one. Don't fight it. Factorize the two out of every term first, and complete the square inside the bracket exactly as before. Half of five over two is five over four; square it, add and subtract. Then the step people forget: multiply the two back into both terms. Minus seventeen over sixteen becomes minus seventeen over eight.

scenes.heading: A negative in front — same recipe

steps.note: Factorize the $-4$ out of every term — the sign travels with it.
Inside: half of 6 is 3, square it: 9. Then $-9 + \tfrac{35}{4} = -\tfrac{1}{4}$.
$-4 \times \left(-\tfrac{1}{4}\right) = +1$. Maximum point $(-3, 1)$ — it opens downwards, and $h = -3$ because the bracket says $x + 3$.

verify.note: the rewrite is the same function

scenes.narration: A negative in front works the same way. Factorize minus four out of every term; the sign travels with it. Inside the bracket, half of six is three, three squared is nine, and minus nine plus thirty-five over four is minus a quarter. Multiply minus four back in: minus four times minus a quarter is plus one. Maximum point: minus three, one. Notice the h is minus three, because the bracket says x plus three.

scenes.prompt: Your turn — a real prelim question (Crescent Girls 2023). Factorize the $-3$ out, complete the square inside, multiply back. Type the turning point as $(h, k)$.
scenes.why: $-3x^2 + 12x - 4 = -3(x-2)^2 + 8$, so the turning point is $(2, 8)$ — a maximum, because $a = -3 < 0$.
scenes.narration: Your turn, on a real prelim question. Factorize the minus three out, complete the square inside, and multiply back. Then type the turning point as h comma k.

scenes.heading: Proving a quadratic is always positive
scenes.intro: Show that $x^2 - 4x + 7$ is positive for all real values of $x$.

steps.note: Half of $-4$ is $-2$; square it: $4$. Add and subtract.
A square is never negative — so the whole thing is at least 3. That one line is the proof examiners want.

verify.note: the rewrite is the same function

scenes.narration: Now the other exam favourite: show that a quadratic is always positive. Complete the square: x minus two, all squared, plus three. A square can never be negative, so the expression is at least three, which is bigger than zero. That single line is the whole proof.

scenes.heading: The two green lights
scenes.text:
To prove a quadratic is **always positive**: complete the square into $a(x-h)^2 + k$, then check two things — $a > 0$ AND $k > 0$.

Miss either and it isn't. Picture it: the curve opens upwards with its lowest point above the $x$-axis.

Exams flip it too: "never greater than 4" means $a < 0$ with $k = 4$.
scenes.narration: Two green lights, every time. The a must be positive, and the k must be positive. Miss either one and the proof collapses. In picture terms, the curve opens upwards and its lowest point sits above the x-axis. Exams flip it too: never greater than four means a negative a with k equal to four.

scenes.heading: The slip that costs the most marks
scenes.text:
Find the minimum value of $y = x^2 - 4x$: complete the square, $(x-2)^2 - 4$, turning point $(2, -4)$.

The minimum VALUE is $-4$ — the $y$-coordinate. Writing $2$ is the classic slip: $x = 2$ is only *where* it happens.

Say the sentence in full: "minimum value $-4$, when $x = 2$".
scenes.narration: Here's the slip that costs the most marks. Find the minimum value of x squared minus four x. Complete the square: x minus two, squared, minus four. The minimum value is minus four, the y-coordinate, not two. Two is only where it happens. Say the whole sentence: minimum value minus four, when x equals two.

scenes.prompt: Last one (Mayflower 2022). Write it in descending powers first: $-2x^2 + 8x + 5$. Then factorize the $-2$ out, complete the square, multiply back.
scenes.why: $5 + 8x - 2x^2 = -2(x-2)^2 + 13$, so the turning point is $(2, 13)$ — a maximum.
scenes.narration: Last one. Rewrite it in descending powers first, then it's the same three moves: factorize the minus two out, complete the square inside, multiply back. Type the turning point.

scenes.heading: You own the rewrite now
scenes.text:
Half it, square it, add and subtract → bracket → read off $(h, k)$.

That one rewrite answers every classic: turning points, maximum and minimum values, "always positive" proofs, and the word problem asking for the greatest height. Go make it automatic.
scenes.narration: That's the whole topic. Half it, square it, add and subtract, bracket it, read off h and k. One rewrite answers every classic: turning points, greatest and least values, always-positive proofs, and every word problem that asks for a greatest height. Go make it automatic.
